title: *All-inclusive* is a word, not a contract.
subtitle: What it usually covers, what it quietly doesn't, and how to check.

text: The fare isn't the price until you've read the exclusions.
sub: Two sailings at the same headline number can differ by a great deal once the extras land on your onboard account in week two.

title: Four things inclusive fares generally cover

items.head: Dining, including specialty
items.body: On most luxury lines every restaurant is included; on some a reservation limit applies rather than a charge.

items.head: Wines and spirits aboard
items.body: Typically a house selection at lunch and dinner, with a reserve list priced separately.

items.head: Crew gratuities
items.body: Largely a solved problem on an inclusive fare. Worth asking whether it extends to spa and butler.

items.head: Wi-Fi and still water
items.body: Usually one device per suite. A second is often a charge, and speed varies with where you are.

title: Inside the fare vs on the bill
Ask these before you compare two fares

points.label: Air, or no air
points.value: An included-air fare and a cruise-only fare are not comparable. Separate them first.

points.label: Excursions included
points.value: Some lines include one per port, some include none, some include a curated few.

points.label: Transfers and hotels
points.value: Pre-cruise nights and port transfers are the most common quiet omission of the lot.

points.label: What the deposit buys
points.value: Refundable or not. That difference is a real cost and it never appears in the headline.

text: Inclusive is a design decision, not a discount.
sub: The lines that include most are not being generous — they are removing the onboard sell, so nobody spends the week auditing a bill. That is what you are buying.

title: Save this for your next fare comparison
body: Or send me the two fares you're weighing up and I'll tell you, in two lines, which one is actually cheaper.
